title: اختبار تدريبي على اختبار شهر نوفمبر - Science - الصف الأول الإعدادي لغات
scope: November monthly test practice (29/11): from Chemical Bonds to the end of Gravitational Forces.
source: Scope from the science (languages) supervisor, 2026-11-19. All questions from the Performances and Assessments book 2026/2027, Prep 1, Term 1: pp. 25-48.

questions.text: An atom of a metallic element that lost one electron or more.
questions.explanation: A metal atom that loses electrons has more protons than electrons, so it becomes a positive ion, e.g. Na⁺ (p. 44).

questions.text: A bond formed as a result of an electrostatic attraction between a positive ion and a negative ion.
questions.explanation: The ionic bond is the attraction between a cation and an anion, as in sodium chloride (p. 44).

questions.text: A bond formed when each atom shares two electrons.
questions.explanation: Sharing one electron each gives a single bond, two a double bond (as in O₂), three a triple bond (as in N₂) (p. 44).

questions.text: The simplest molecule of an organic compound, in which a carbon atom is bonded to four hydrogen atoms.
questions.explanation: Methane CH₄ is the simplest organic molecule: one carbon atom with four single covalent bonds to hydrogen (p. 44).

questions.text: Arranging some substances according to how easily they lose electrons.
questions.explanation: The electrostatic series arranges substances by how easily they lose electrons when rubbed (p. 32).

questions.text: The device used to measure weak electric charges.
questions.explanation: The coulomb meter measures weak electric charges; the electroscope detects a charge and its type (p. 32).

questions.text: A device used to determine the type of electric charge.
questions.explanation: The electroscope (with a metal disc and gold leaves) detects a charge and determines its type (p. 32).

questions.text: The area surrounding a magnet where its magnetic force appears.
questions.explanation: The magnetic field is the area around a magnet where its effect appears; magnetic field lines are imaginary lines that represent it (p. 35).

questions.text: Materials that are not attracted to magnets.
questions.explanation: Non-magnetic materials such as copper, aluminum, silver and gold are not attracted to magnets (p. 35).

questions.text: Forces that affect objects when they come into contact with each other.
questions.explanation: Contact forces (e.g. collision, elastic and friction forces) act on touch; field forces such as gravity act at a distance (p. 39-40).

questions.text: When an ebonite rod is rubbed with a piece of wool, the rod gains a ...... charge, while the piece of wool gains a ...... charge.
questions.explanation: Electrons move from the wool to the ebonite: the ebonite gains electrons (negative) and the wool loses them (positive) (p. 30).

questions.text: Electric force lines start from the ...... charge and end at the ...... charge.
questions.explanation: Electric force lines are imaginary, do not intersect, start at the positive charge and end at the negative charge (p. 31).

questions.text: In electrostatic painting, the object to be painted is charged with a ...... charge and the paint spray with a ...... charge.
questions.explanation: Opposite charges attract, so the paint spreads evenly on the object and less paint is wasted (p. 31).

questions.text: The magnetic force is strongest at ...... of the magnet.
questions.explanation: Iron filings gather in large quantities at the two poles, where the magnetic force is strongest (p. 36-37).

questions.text: Magnetic field lines emerge from the ...... pole toward the ...... pole.
questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines start at the north pole and end at the south pole, and condense at the poles (p. 37).

questions.text: An object with a mass of 500 g has a weight of ...... newtons. (Gravitational field intensity = 10 N/kg)
questions.explanation: 500 g = 0.5 kg. Weight = mass × gravitational field intensity = 0.5 × 10 = 5 N (p. 41).

questions.text: An object weighing 50 newtons has a mass of ...... kg. (Gravitational field intensity = 10 N/kg)
questions.explanation: Mass = weight ÷ gravitational field intensity = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 kg (p. 41).

questions.text: By increasing the distance between two objects, the force of attraction between them ......
questions.explanation: Gravitational force increases with the masses of the two objects and decreases as the distance between them increases (p. 40).

questions.text: The movement of the Moon around the Earth is an example of ...... motion.
questions.explanation: Orbital motion is the motion of an object in a curved path around another central object, like the Moon around the Earth or electrons around the nucleus (p. 40).

questions.text: The bond in the oxygen molecule is a double covalent bond, because ......
choices: it forms between a positive ion and a negative ion
each oxygen atom shares one electron with the other atom
each oxygen atom shares two electrons with the other atom
one oxygen atom gives two electrons to the other
questions.explanation: Each oxygen atom needs two electrons to complete its outer level, so the two atoms share two pairs of electrons (p. 26).

questions.text: The bond in sodium chloride is ionic, because ......
choices: sodium and chlorine share one electron each
both atoms gain electrons and become negative ions
sodium and chlorine share two electrons each
sodium loses an electron and becomes a positive ion, chlorine gains it and becomes a negative ion, and the two ions attract
questions.explanation: Sodium (a metal) loses one electron and chlorine (a non-metal) gains it; the electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ is the ionic bond (p. 26).

questions.text: Ionic compounds are electrically neutral, because ......
choices: the total positive charges equal the total negative charges
questions.explanation: In an ionic compound the charges of the cations and the anions cancel out (p. 46).

questions.text: Metal chains hang from fuel tank trucks and touch the ground, in order to ......
choices: discharge the static electric charges into the ground and prevent sparks
keep the truck balanced on the road
questions.explanation: Friction produces static charges on the tank; the metal chains conduct them to the ground so no spark ignites the fuel (p. 29-30).

questions.text: Compass cases are made of copper or plastic, not iron, because ......
choices: copper and plastic are non-magnetic, so they do not affect the movement of the needle
copper and plastic attract the needle to the north
copper and plastic are magnetic materials
questions.explanation: The compass needle is a free-moving magnet; an iron case would attract it and spoil the direction (p. 36).

questions.text: The weight of an object on the Earth's surface is greater than its weight on the Moon's surface, because ......
choices: the Moon is farther from the Sun
there is no gravity on the Moon
the Earth's gravitational field is stronger than the Moon's
the mass of the object on the Earth is greater
questions.explanation: Mass stays the same, but weight = mass × gravitational field intensity, and the Moon's field is about 1/6 of the Earth's (p. 40).

questions.text: What happens when you rub two ebonite rods with a piece of silk and bring them close to each other?
choices: They repel, because they carry similar (negative) charges
Nothing happens, because they are not charged
They attract, because they carry different charges
questions.explanation: Both rods gain electrons from the silk and become negative; similar charges repel (p. 32).

questions.text: What happens when you hang an ebonite rod rubbed with silk and bring close to it a glass rod rubbed with silk?
choices: They repel, because both are negative
They repel, because both are positive
They attract, because the ebonite is negative and the glass is positive
questions.explanation: Rubbed with silk, glass loses electrons (positive) and ebonite gains electrons (negative); different charges attract (p. 32).

questions.text: What happens when you touch the disc of a charged electroscope with your hand?
choices: The gold leaves collapse, because the charges pass through the body to the ground
The charge on the disc doubles
questions.explanation: Your body is a conductor, so the charge escapes to the ground and the leaves close (p. 32).

questions.text: What happens when a negatively charged ebonite rod is brought near the disc of a negatively charged electroscope?
choices: The divergence of the gold leaves increases
The divergence of the gold leaves decreases
questions.explanation: A charge of the same type as the electroscope's increases the divergence; an opposite charge decreases it (p. 32).

questions.text: What happens when a single magnet is broken into several pieces?
choices: Each piece has one pole only
Each piece becomes a new magnet with a north pole and a south pole
questions.explanation: It is impossible to get a single magnetic pole: every piece is a complete magnet (p. 34).

questions.text: What happens when the south pole of a magnet is brought close to the north pole of a freely suspended magnet?
choices: The suspended magnet loses its magnetism
questions.explanation: Law of attraction and repulsion: different magnetic poles attract, similar poles repel (p. 36).

questions.text: What happens to the gravitational force between two objects when their masses increase?
choices: It changes into a repulsion force
questions.explanation: Gravitational force increases as the masses of the two objects increase (p. 40).

questions.text: Electric force lines are imaginary and intersect with each other.
questions.explanation: False. Electric force lines are imaginary, but they never intersect (p. 28).

questions.text: Magnetic field lines condense at the poles and diverge as they move away from them.
questions.explanation: True. That is why the magnetic force is strongest at the poles (p. 34).

questions.text: The mass of an object changes from one planet to another.
questions.explanation: False. The mass is constant everywhere; it is the weight that changes from one planet to another (p. 39-40).

questions.text: Nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials.
questions.explanation: True. Iron, nickel and cobalt are attracted to magnets (p. 36).

questions.text: The bond in the hydrogen molecule is a single covalent bond.
questions.explanation: True. Each hydrogen atom shares one electron (H─H) (p. 73).

questions.text: Compared with its atom, a positive ion has ...... electrons, while a negative ion has ...... electrons.
questions.explanation: A positive ion lost electrons and a negative ion gained electrons; the number of protons does not change (p. 26 and 45).

questions.text: Which of these describes most ionic compounds compared with covalent compounds?
choices: They have lower boiling points than covalent compounds
They dissolve in water, conduct electricity, and have high melting and boiling points
They do not dissolve in water and have low melting points
They do not conduct electricity in solution
questions.explanation: Most covalent compounds do not dissolve in water, do not conduct electricity, and have low melting and boiling points (p. 26).

questions.text: Mass is measured in ...... and is constant, while weight is measured in ...... and changes from place to place.
questions.explanation: Weight is measured with a spring balance in newtons; mass in kilograms (p. 39 and 41).

questions.text: How can you infer the type of charge on a charged rod?
choices: Bring it near the disc of an electroscope with a known charge and watch the gold leaves
Weigh it with a spring balance
questions.explanation: If the divergence increases, the rod has the same type of charge as the electroscope; if it decreases, the opposite type (p. 31-32).

questions.text: How can you infer that a metal coin contains a magnetic material such as nickel?
choices: Put it in water: it sinks
Bring a magnet close to it: it is attracted
Rub it with wool: it becomes charged
questions.explanation: Only magnetic materials are attracted to a magnet; a copper-nickel coin is attracted because of the nickel (p. 33).

questions.text: How can you infer the shape of the magnetic field around a bar magnet?
choices: Scatter iron filings around it: they arrange along the magnetic field lines
Measure it with a coulomb meter
questions.explanation: Iron filings line up along the field lines and gather most densely at the poles (p. 34-35).
